I think as the Republican selection of a speaker settles down and as committees are chosen, you're going to see the House, which is going to become an effective barrier in a lot of respect to major legislative initiatives from the left. You're also going to see a potential for a rethinking of the house as a legislative body. For too long, basically a strong speaker system has existed that has allowed Nancy Pelosi and others to function effectively as a lot of crowds. I think you're also going to see, you're probably not going to see a budget pass, both houses, although you have Mr. Boyle, and Mr. Spock are both in critical positions in the house on this. turn_text: But that's very interesting. And Alex, as a former congressional staffer, how do you see Washington functioning with a greater emphasis on the committees and a greater emphasis on that kind of incremental improvement that the congressmen spoke of?

Well, maybe I hope my optimism isn't misplaced, but I often found that when There is really a lot of focus on committee work, which is often behind the scenes. It's not as high profile. You're working very closely both at the staff level, at the member level, and at the chairman level. Oftentimes, you're working very closely, really getting into the weeds and the nuts and bolts of the legislation, and going through that process you know, I found could often create a more positive working environment. You're trying to get bills moving. You're sort of forced, oftentimes forced to compromise. And even for those, you know, for whom, you know,

luck in to do that. If you're forced into it, it can, you know, you'll create a more positive work environment and that can kind of lead into more productivity at the, you know, once bills get to the floor, once they're, you know, going back and forth between the chambers. So, you know, I happen to think a committee process if, you know, if the chairs and the senior staff are setting the right tone can really be very positive for the institution overall.

That makes a lot of sense to me. And one of the frustrations we're going to see coming out of this Congress is there are going to be some very big issues that are going to be very hard to move forward. Immigration is a good example. I find it very hard to envision major legislation that fundamentally changes the immigration laws in a way that more and more people acknowledge has to happen, happening in the next two years, even at a time when we're clearly having a crisis on the southern border, at least. I think you're probably going to see a great deal of difficulty moving serious tax reform at a time like this, simply because I don't think this treasury really has a deep instinct for tax reform. I think ideologically the current administration probably doesn't function that way. But I do think there is a potential to develop tax reform for the future in the guts of the committee's Senate Finance and House Ways and Means. There are going to be some other issues that I think are not going to go forward that are going to really frustrate people. And one of them, I think, is national defense. I am hoping that we're going to see a major investment in our national defense and a particular investment in improving the technology of our armed forces. I don't know that we have the will to do that. And the big issue hanging over all of this, which is a distinct change from the environment of the last couple of years, I think there's a growing recognition that our national debt is out of control, that our deficits have not been rained in, that our budget process is broken. And in order to dig our way out from under this, on the lessons of history, we need to grow the economy faster. And I don't think there's a real consensus between the Republicans and Democrats on precisely how to do that. Very proud of the fact that the Chamber has made a particular focus on economic growth.

But I think in general, there's a recognition that we need a stronger, more consistent trade policy. And there are going to be opportunities. I think the new Indo-Pacific economic framework has the potential to produce some very fertile changes in trade policy that I think could be very, very significant for the long haul. I think if they're given the green light, they have the potential to move forward and make real progress in this space. When we saw the environmental initiatives passed by Congress last time, largely incentives for new green technologies, they had significant domestic preferences. built into them as tax provisions. Those have been partially waived vis-a-vis Europe, but not completely. And I think those things are going to continue to be a potential irritant, particularly because of the priority that the administration places not only on trade, but also on climate change initiatives. I don't know how Alex feels about this, but I think trade is one of the areas where there could be a certain level of bipartisanship and potentially some very new policies.

turn_text: Congressman, I certainly hope you're right there. I completely agree that trade ought to be a priority of the administration and the new Congress. The United States has trade agreements with maybe 20 countries, but it's been at least a decade since a new free trade agreement has been signed. by the United States. And of course, we don't exist in a vacuum. Other countries, the EU, China, even Mexico and Canada, other allies, but all these countries are pursuing trade agreements around the globe. I think we trail all those countries and the EU in terms of trade agreements with other countries. And we're losing opportunity. Pennsylvania companies, we've shown when they have the opportunity to compete with with, you know, around the globe, they succeed. But we need, you know, we need good trade agreements that promote fair and free trade in order to do that. And certainly hope it is a priority going into the next couple of years.

The other big issue, of course, is the World Trade Organization, which has fallen on, I think, rough times. I think the participation in the world trading system by the United States is facilitated when you have a strong rules-based trading system. And what we're seeing right now is a bifurcation where increasingly we have countries that are aligned with us that are following the same general rules And at the same time, we are seeing organized more and more around China, another axis that approaches trade in a very different way. And increasingly, I think, a mutually exclusive way. And that is going to be one of the most difficult nuts that this administration in the next few is going to have to crack. The World Trade Organization is going to have to be rethought if it's going to be the center of a rules-based trading system. I think that we allowed China into the WTO when I was in Congress. And we had no notion at the time that China at this stage would still be insisting on being treated as a developing economy, essentially dictating for itself a series of exclusions from the rules that the developed world is required to follow. That is precisely the kind of inequity that needs to be rethought. And if we're going to have a strong rules-based trading system, there needs to be an accepted rule keeper that's able to make decisions that countries will abide by. That means the WTO is going to have to be reformed or replaced.

turn_text: So taking a little turn here, let's talk about Harrisburg. We've seen an unprecedented move in leadership over the last 24 hours or so. Probably the best way to lead into this is kind of have Alex walk through what happened and then we can talk a little bit about what the implications are.

Yeah, with everything going on in Washington, DC, if you thought you were going to get anything more predictable and conventional in Harrisburg, you are mistaken. It has been an interesting period of leadership elections in particular. And it has been a couple of months, really, since the November election, when there has been a tremendous intrigue into how leadership elections and the Speaker of the House in Pennsylvania in particular was going to play out. Democrats on election night won a very narrow majority, 102 to 101, first majority for the Democratic Party in over a decade. But soon thereafter, they became a functional minority, the unfortunate unfortunate death of a state representative Tony DeLuca out in Allegheny County, a couple members of the House Democratic Caucus elected to higher offices. So when the election for Speaker of the House came up, it was 101 Republicans, 299 Democrats, and certainly not clear how that election was going to play out. Joanna McClinton from Philadelphia, the Democratic leader was viewed as the front runner for Speaker of the House, but not necessarily a clear path to get there, given how the votes were shaking out. Brian Cutler, the former Speaker of the House from Lancaster County and the Republican leader sort of viewed as the Republican alternative. Ultimately, when the final vote came up, neither of them were part of that election. two names that had really not been discussed much at all were on that, you know, in the final vote. On the Republican side, you had State Representative Carl Metzger from Somerset County, and on the Democratic side, State Representative Mark Rossi from Berks County, and Representative Rossi all ultimately won the election as Speaker of the House for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, with the coalition vote of all the Democrats and about 15 or so Republicans, including Republican leadership, who voted for Mark Rossi. And if you had asked most political prognosticators in Pennsylvania, who was going to be Speaker of the House at the end of January 3rd, I certainly didn't hear many mentioning Mark Rossi. And yet, here we are. So it'll be very interesting to see, of course, kind of how things play out in the days, weeks and months ahead. There will be special elections eventually to fill those open seats and expected that at some point, Democrats will have a functional majority potentially. But on the other hand, Mark, representative Mark Rossi, now Speaker Rossi, after being elected, told his colleagues that he planned to serve as an independent and not caucus with the Democratic Party, which is, you know, kind of an unprecedented move in the history of Pennsylvania. So, yeah, a lot of moving pieces and a lot of interesting developments here in Harrisburgville.
